name: Metformin
lead: Metformin, sold under the brand name Glucophage among others, is a biguanide medication taken by mouth and the main first-line drug for type 2 diabetes, particularly in people who are overweight.[1] It is also used in polycystic ovary syndrome (which Wikipedia terms polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome) and sometimes off-label to limit metabolic effects of antipsychotic drugs.[1] It was first described in the scientific literature in 1922 by Emil Werner and James Bell, studied in humans by the French physician Jean Sterne in the 1950s, and introduced as a medication in France in 1957.[1] It is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines and in 2023 was the third most commonly prescribed medication in the United States.[1]

Metformin is discussed in longevity and body-composition communities because observational studies in diabetics have linked it to lower cancer risk and mortality, and because its proposed mechanisms (AMPK activation, effects on mTOR signalling, reduced insulin) overlap with those studied in ageing research.[2][3][4] Whether it slows ageing in people without diabetes is unproven, and reviews published in 2021 and 2025 take a cautious or critical view of the evidence.[5][6]

It is a prescription drug in the US, UK and EU. Some forum members report using it off-label or obtaining it from overseas pharmacies, and discussions on T Nation link it to blood sugar management during testosterone replacement or growth hormone use and to belly fat.[7][8] Metformin has no established role as an appearance treatment.
infobox: Prescription-only; generic; on WHO Essential Medicines list

paras: The American Diabetes Association and the American College of Physicians recommend metformin as a first-line agent for type 2 diabetes, and it is as effective as repaglinide and more effective than other oral drugs according to Wikipedia.[1] A 2020 Annals of Internal Medicine network meta-analysis compared benefits and harms of glucose-lowering drugs.[9] The UKPDS 34 trial reported that intensive blood-glucose control with metformin affected complications in overweight patients with type 2 diabetes,[10] and a 10-year follow-up of intensive glucose control was published in 2008.[11] A 2006 trial compared the durability of glycaemic control with rosiglitazone, metformin and glyburide.[12]

In prediabetes, the Diabetes Prevention Program found in 2002 that lifestyle intervention or metformin reduced the incidence of type 2 diabetes,[13] and a 10-year follow-up reported on diabetes incidence and weight loss.[14] A 2019 systematic review summarised by Wikipedia found moderate-quality evidence that metformin reduced diabetes risk compared with placebo or usual diet and exercise, but not compared with intensive diet or exercise.[1]

subs.h: Polycystic ovary syndrome and other uses
paras: Wikipedia describes tentative evidence that metformin raises live birth rates in PCOS, including women who did not conceive with clomiphene.[1] A 2024 meta-analysis compared metformin with combined oral contraceptive pills,[15] 2023 and 2024 meta-analyses evaluated inositol as an alternative,[16][17] and a 2019 meta-analysis compared GLP-1 receptor agonists with metformin in PCOS.[18] Metformin has also been compared with insulin in gestational diabetes in a 2008 New England Journal of Medicine trial and a 2021 randomised trial,[19][20] and Wikipedia notes good short-term safety but unclear long-term safety for mother and child.[1] It is associated with weight loss in obesity without diabetes and with counteracting weight gain from olanzapine and clozapine.[1]

Interest in metformin as an anti-ageing drug stems from observational data such as a 2005 BMJ study reporting reduced cancer risk in diabetic patients taking it,[21] and from laboratory findings that it affects pathways linked to ageing. A 2020 Cell Metabolism review argues metformin attenuates several hallmarks of ageing,[3] whereas a 2021 critical review in Frontiers in Endocrinology examined whether the evidence supports it as an anti-ageing drug,[6] and a 2025 review in Ageing Research Reviews describes emerging uncertainty about its anti-ageing potential.[5] A large randomised trial of metformin in about 3,000 people aged 65 to 79 without glucose intolerance, testing whether it can prevent or reverse age-associated disease and disability, was described as ongoing in a 2024 review.[22]
No controlled study found testing metformin for skin, hair or facial appearance in healthy people. Its main appearance-related use is for weight and metabolic effects, as in PCOS.

Metformin lowers blood glucose by decreasing glucose production in the liver, increasing insulin sensitivity in tissues, and, according to Wikipedia, raising secretion of GDF15, which reduces appetite.[1] A 2001 study identified activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) as part of its mechanism,[23] an enzyme that senses energy status and interacts with NAD+ metabolism and SIRT1 activity.[24] A 2000 paper provided evidence that metformin inhibits complex 1 of the mitochondrial respiratory chain,[25] and Grokipedia also lists effects on intestinal glucose absorption and the gut microbiome.[26] A randomised trial reported that metformin changes gut microbiome composition and circulating short-chain fatty acids.[27] mTOR and HIF-1alpha signalling are involved in the metabolic basis of trained immunity in a 2014 Science paper listed among metformin literature.[28]

The most common adverse effects are gastrointestinal: diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, cramps and flatulence, most frequent when starting or increasing the dose. Wikipedia says about 5 percent of people cannot tolerate it even at low doses and that slow or extended-release preparations can improve tolerability.[1] Reviews describe how metformin acts on the gastrointestinal tract and how intolerance may be overcome.[29][30]

Long-term use is associated with lower vitamin B12 and higher homocysteine, and some researchers recommend screening; the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study reported a link between long-term metformin use and B12 deficiency.[1][31] Lactic acidosis is rare and linked to impaired liver or kidney function; the US label carries a boxed warning, and Wikipedia states the FDA recommends avoiding metformin at eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.[1][32] Metformin carries a small risk of hypoglycaemia, usually with intense exercise, calorie deficit or other glucose-lowering drugs.[1] Contraindications include severe renal impairment, hypersensitivity and metabolic acidosis.[1] Pregnancy data have not linked metformin to a clear increase in major birth defects.[32]

Well-powered randomised trials establish metformin's role in glycaemic control, prediabetes and pregnancy-related uses; see the Diabetes Prevention Program,[13] UKPDS 34,[10] and the metformin versus insulin gestational diabetes trial.[19] Trials of combination therapy include metformin with atorvastatin in diabetes and dyslipidaemia (ATOMIC)[33] and initial combination of empagliflozin and metformin.[34]

In ageing, the available human evidence is mainly observational data from diabetics and small mechanistic studies, and reviews published in 2021 and 2025 describe the case for a lifespan or healthspan benefit as uncertain.[5][6] A randomised trial in cancer survivors who were overweight or obese examined effects of metformin and behavioural weight loss on the gut microbiome.[27] Registered studies include metformin for insulin resistance in hepatitis C (n=126),[35] a trial of metformin plus clomiphene for ovulation induction in insulin-resistant PCOS (n=388, terminated),[36] and a study in obesity,[37] along with numerous bioequivalence studies.[38]
No clinical study was found testing metformin for appearance outcomes in people without a metabolic indication.

Metformin derives from guanidine compounds found in the plant Galega officinalis (goat's rue), long used in herbal medicine for diabetes-like symptoms. It was synthesised in the 1920s, set aside after insulin became available, re-evaluated in the 1940s and brought into clinical use in France in 1957 after Jean Sterne's work.[1][26] The FDA approved it in 1994 according to Grokipedia.[26] The UKPDS results in 1998 gave major support to its use in overweight type 2 diabetes,[10] and the Diabetes Prevention Program in 2002 supported its use in prediabetes.[13]

On T Nation, members mention metformin in several roles. Some describe taking it after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis and ask whether it affects muscle gain,[39][40] others report using it at 1,000 mg per day with no side effects alongside testosterone replacement therapy and say their carbohydrate sensitivity improved,[41] a physician reportedly agreed it might help belly fat during TRT,[42] and a post on obtaining it from overseas pharmacies without a prescription appears in discussion of blood-sugar control during growth hormone use.[7][8] One member said he had read on the forum that metformin inhibits muscle growth in a statistically significant way after about 18 months of daily use.[40] Posts like these are personal reports and not controlled data. No looksmax.org or Reddit material was identified.

timeline.event: Emil Werner and James Bell first describe metformin in the scientific literature.[1]
Metformin is introduced as a medication in France.[1]
UKPDS 34 reports on metformin in overweight type 2 diabetes patients.[10]
Diabetes Prevention Program reports reduced diabetes incidence with metformin or lifestyle intervention.[13]
A review describes emerging uncertainty about metformin's anti-ageing potential.[5]

lore.intro: On T Nation metformin comes up mostly as a diabetes drug taken by members, as an add-on to testosterone or growth hormone use, and in debates about whether it limits muscle growth.[40][41][7]

claims.claim: Metformin slows ageing and extends lifespan
claims.believers: Longevity enthusiasts cite observational links to lower cancer and mortality in diabetics and mechanistic work on AMPK and mTOR.[21][3]
claims.experts: A 2021 critical review and a 2025 review describe the case for metformin as an anti-ageing drug as uncertain, and a large trial in older adults without diabetes was described as ongoing.[5][6][22]

claims.claim: Metformin helps with belly fat and carbohydrate sensitivity
claims.believers: A T Nation member on TRT reports improved carb sensitivity at 1,000 mg per day, and another says a doctor agreed it might help belly fat.[41][42]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states metformin is typically associated with weight loss and may help in obesity without diabetes; it is also associated with GI side effects.[1]

claims.believers: A T Nation member who has taken a large daily dose for about 18 months reports reading that metformin inhibits muscle growth in a statistically significant manner.[40] Another asks how its insulin-sensitising effect relates to building muscle.[39]
claims.experts: Reviews of anti-ageing potential describe the human data as uncertain; no study cited in this article directly settles the question for lifters.[5]

claims.claim: Metformin from overseas pharmacies is a way to manage blood sugar during hormone use
claims.believers: Members describe buying it without a prescription from foreign pharmacies for use alongside testosterone or growth hormone.[7][8]
claims.experts: Metformin is a prescription-only drug in the US with a boxed warning for lactic acidosis in the label for combination products and contraindication in severe renal impairment.[32][1]

claims.claim: Long-term metformin can cause vitamin B12 deficiency
claims.believers: Forum members ask whether B12 should be supplemented, and one reports taking a multivitamin.[41]
claims.experts: The Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study and Wikipedia report an association between long-term use and B12 deficiency, and some researchers recommend screening.[31][1]
